cells.tense: Something is finishing, and you are standing where it finishes.
cells.act: notice what is newly here, right now
cells.ask: Once today, take in something that wasn't here a month ago. Give it as long as it needs to register, then go on with what you were doing.
cells.core:
Something is finishing, and you're standing while it finishes, able to say what it was and what it's turning into. That isn't a small thing. Most people either slam the door or act like nothing closed. You can name what ended and still leave the next thing room to arrive. When that works, the fair thing becomes visible without effort: the scales settle, the accounts read level, and the next piece has somewhere to land.

The bend is subtler. Still holding the pen over the last page, you keep half a hand on it — reading the ending well enough, but not quite turning. Take in what's here now, once, before the day moves. Notice what's different from a month ago; let that register before you carry on. The door doesn't need pushing. It needs you to see it's open.
cells.sheetLine: You can name what ended and still leave room for what's coming.
cells.verb: Closing a cycle and letting the next one start
cells.place: Where what's owed is weighed and set level again

cells.tense: The ending has been written in advance, and you are already living past it.
cells.act: open the door to the next thing on time, not early
cells.ask: Before you call the next thing finished, sit with it a day. Check whether it actually is — and let what's true decide, not the plan.
cells.core:
You're good at this, and the skill is the problem right now: you can see how a thing ends so clearly that you've already moved past it, living in a next that hasn't actually started. The version where it's done is running before the work is. So the endings come early — announced, wrapped, marked complete — and the actual last stretch gets skipped, the piece that only happens in real time.

That's where fair weight goes out of true: one side of the scale is holding a future, and the other has nothing on it yet. Before you call the next thing finished, give it a day. Sit with it that long, then check whether it truly is closed. Not everything you can look past is behind you.

What arrives meets a person who's actually here, not one already gone.
cells.sheetLine: You see the ending so early you sometimes move past one you haven't reached.
cells.verb: Closing a cycle and letting the next one start
cells.place: Where what's owed is weighed and set level again

cells.tense: The last door is still open, and you haven't walked back through it.
cells.act: receive the thing that is coming instead of bracing for it
cells.ask: When something new shows up, take a piece of it before you grade it. An offer, an opening, an invitation — let that much land whether or not it counts.
cells.core:
You still show up, you still start things, and you know the way through the middle of a cycle. What's stopped is the closing. A door stays open at your back, so everything since has been partial by comparison, and each new thing gets met at arm's length before it has a chance to be real. The searching continues because nothing has been allowed to finish.

Meet what's coming as it comes. If it's an offer, take a piece of it. If it's an invitation, go and sit among the people. Let it land before you grade it. What's entering is already here; the work is putting your hands under it. Then the scales have something to weigh again — not a past you're still holding open against a present you haven't let touch you.
cells.sheetLine: Nothing has been allowed to finish, so nothing new quite lands.
cells.verb: Closing a cycle and letting the next one start
cells.place: Where what's owed is weighed and set level again

cells.tense: You are managing an ending that is already over, treating it as though it were still in progress.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Find the thing you're still managing that's already over. Tell no one. Set it down, and watch what happens next.
cells.core:
There's a job here you're still doing, competently, that may be finished. Or not — the trouble is you'd be the last to know, because the pen is in your hand and the turn doesn't get written down. You keep working an account that may have already closed, and there's no way to feel which it is from inside the doing.

So test it with your hands. Stop handling that one thing and set it down — not forever, a week — without telling anyone. No announcement, no ceremony, no handing it off. Leave your hands empty and see what actually breaks. The scale you thought you were holding level will either move or hold its own weight. Either way, you'll know something you didn't know. And what's over can be over, which is not a loss.
cells.sheetLine: You keep managing something that may already be over.
cells.verb: Closing a cycle and letting the next one start
cells.place: Where what's owed is weighed and set level again
